newsitem.title: USA: Oil imports drive October wholesale inventories up.
newsitem.headline: Oil imports drive October wholesale inventories up.

text.p: A surge in petroleum imports during October helped drive wholesalers' inventories higher, the Commerce Department said Tuesday, as stocks were built up for the winter heating season.
Overall inventories held by merchant wholesalers climbed 0.6 percent during October to a seasonally adjusted $258.6 billion after falling 0.6 percent in September.

All the increase occurred among nondurable goods, ranging from paper to food and chemicals, but the biggest gain was an 8.2 percent jump in petroleum stocks to a value of $16 billion. That followed a slight 0.6 percent rise in September.
Monthly trade reports from Commerce had previously indicated that both the price and volume of petroleum imports were rising, so the pickup in stocks was not surprising.
Inventories of all types of nondurables climbed 2 percent to $94.9 billion during October after dropping 2.2 percent in September.
By contrast, inventories of costly and long-lasting durable items like cars, hardware and production machinery eased 0.1 percent to $163.7 billion after a slim 0.2 percent September increase.
Wholesale sales increased moderately during October by 0.3 percent to $202 billion, less than half the 0.7 percent rise posted in September.

Sales of automotive products, which represents deliveries to dealers, dropped 1.1 percent to $16.9 billion after a 2.8 percent September jump. Strikes in Canada against industry leader General Motors Corp. disrupted U.S. production in October by causing parts shortages that affected the supply of popular models.

But there also were sales declines from September for products like furniture, electrical goods and hardware. The housing industry has been slowing -- both construction and sales -- and analysts say suppliers are keeping inventories lean as a result.
